name: Reactance
description: When people feel their freedom or autonomy is being threatened, they resist, push back, or sometimes do the opposite of what is being urged. Pressure can reduce compliance precisely because it feels controlling.
design_relevance_note: Directly relevant to persuasive-design ethics, dark patterns, nagging pop-ups, coercive consent flows, guilt copy, forced continuity, and any interface that tries to push behavior so hard that users resist or rebel.
prevalence_note: Highly relevant in consent, conversion-copy, push-notification, and dark-pattern ethics work; the term is somewhat more academic than the everyday design symptom, but the underlying concept is central to persuasive-design backfire discussions.

findings.description: A meta-analytic review of 20 studies supported psychological reactance as a measurable response to persuasive pressure, best modeled as an intertwined latent state indicated by anger and counterarguing. This gives direct peer-reviewed backing to the claim that autonomy-threatening persuasion can systematically provoke resistance rather than compliance.
findings.source_title: The Nature of Psychological Reactance Revisited: A Meta-Analytic Review

applications.title: Blinkist's paywall disguising its close button as a back button
applications.description: In an early trial-paywall design, Blinkist hid the paywall's exit option by presenting it as a back button rather than a clearly visible close control -- constraining the user's obvious path to decline, which the source frames as triggering resistance rather than encouraging genuine conversion.
applications.ethical_note: Disguising an exit control specifically to make it harder to find is a recognized dark-pattern shape (obstruction), not merely an aggressive-but-honest paywall -- distinct from the Goal Gradient Effect entry from this same underlying redesign project, which represents what the team apparently changed toward afterward.

applications.title: Clubhouse's excessive daily notifications triggering users to disable them entirely
applications.description: Clubhouse sent more than 20 notifications a day, many unrelated to a user's actual follows or interests -- rather than increasing engagement, the volume triggered a sense of lost control that led many users to disable notifications altogether, undermining the app's own engagement goal.
applications.ethical_note: Not a deceptive pattern, but a real disregard for user preference in service of engagement volume -- sending notifications unrelated to what a user actually follows treats attention as available to claim rather than something to earn, which is why this is graded mixed rather than not_applicable despite no dishonesty being involved.

applications.title: GoDaddy's checkout upsell sequence triggering resistance rather than compliance
applications.description: GoDaddy's checkout flow layers confusing domain-protection upsells, fear-based hacking warnings, pre-selected add-on defaults, and a surprise 2-year billing default -- described as producing emotional fatigue and resistance once a user recognizes the pattern, rather than the intended additional purchases.
applications.ethical_note: This is a compound dark-pattern case rather than a single technique -- fear-based messaging, pre-selected defaults, and a hidden billing term stacked together -- and belongs directly alongside this corpus's existing Dark Patterns & Design Ethics literature. The reactance angle specifically documents a real cost to the company itself (user resistance and distrust), a useful counterpoint to any argument that manipulative checkout design is simply effective.
